en: I worship Hari, who is the form of the illustrious Nārāyaṇa, the great abode of the eight syllables, the realization of the Self established through the experience of one's own nature. Oṃ! "May my speech be in my mind"—thus [ends] the peace invocation.
The First Chapter.

Oṃ! The Brahman-puruṣa is inner bliss, whose nature is the Praṇava. The Praṇava consists of three syllables—*a*, *u*, and *m*. This is indeed "Oṃ. By uttering this, the yogi is liberated from the bondage of birth and saṃsāra. Oṃ, salutations to Nārāyaṇa, the bearer of the conch, the discus, and the mace; therefore, the worshiper of the mantra "Oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya" shall go to the abode of Vaikuṇṭha. || 1 ||
Now, as for this city of Brahman, which is like a lotus, it shines with the brilliance of lightning, like a lamp. ||2||
The son of Devakī is devoted to Brahman; Madhusūdana is devoted to Brahman; the lotus-eyed one is devoted to Brahman; Viṣṇu, the infallible, is devoted to Brahman. ||3||
Om! Nārāyaṇa, the one who dwells within all beings, the causal Person, the non-causal, the Supreme Brahman. 4.

Freed from sorrow and delusion, one who meditates upon Viṣṇu does not perish. Non-duality with duality is fearlessness; he who perceives here as if there were multiplicity goes from death to death. (5)
Everything that is within the center of the heart-lotus is established in consciousness; the world has consciousness as its eye, consciousness is its foundation, and consciousness is Brahman. 6.
Having departed from this world by means of this intelligent self, and having attained all desires in that heavenly world, he became immortal—he became immortal. ||7||

In that world where light is eternal, in that world which is most venerable, grant me a place—apart from my own self—in that imperishable and unchanging world; and may he attain immortality. Om. Salutations. 8.
The Second Chapter.

I am one whose own māyā has dissolved; I am the mere reality of the form of incomparable vision; I am one in whom the sense of "I" (ahaṃtā) has set; I am one for whom the distinction between the world, the Lord, and the individual soul (jīva) has dissolved. || 1 ||

I am the Supreme, non-different from the inner self; I am one for whom all injunctions and prohibitions have been utterly destroyed; I am free from the exhaustion of the stages of life (āśramas); I am indeed the expansive consciousness full of bliss. 2.
I am the witness; I am independent; I am established in my own majesty; I am immovable; I am undecaying; I am imperishable; I am devoid of distinctions such as friend and foe. || 3 ||
I am whose sole essence is awakening; I am indeed the singular ocean of the bliss of liberation. I am subtle, I am imperishable, I am the absolute Self with the net of qualities dissolved.
I am the state beyond the three qualities; I am the creator of the many worlds situated within my womb; I am the immutable consciousness; I am the abode of actionlessness; I am inconceivable. || 5 ||
I am one, I am undivided, I am indeed the very form of stainless Nirvāṇa; I am without parts, I am unborn, I am composed of the essence of pure Being alone.
I am my own infinite consciousness; I am of most auspicious nature; I am indivisible; I am all-pervading; I am faultless; I am the mere reality that is boundless and limitless. (7)

I am the one to be known; I am the goal reached by those [who have attained it]; I am the one to be propitiated; I am beloved by all the worlds. I am a mass of supreme bliss; I am the singular ground of supreme bliss. (8)
I am pure, I am non-dual, I am the eternal being, I am devoid of beginning; I have stilled the three limits, I am both bound and liberated, I am the wondrous Self.

I am pure, I am internal, I am the self whose nature is the single flavor of eternal consciousness; I am the purified supreme reality, I am indeed the singular embodiment of the bliss of awakening. 10.
Through the intellect endowed with discernment and reasoning, I know the non-dual Self; nevertheless, the worldly convention of bondage, liberation, and so forth is still perceived.
Even though the phenomenal world has ceased for me, it always appears as if real; just as the reality of the rope persists in the case of a snake and so forth, there is only the reality of Brahman.
Therefore, the world does not exist as something separate from its nature as the substratum of phenomenal manifestation; rather, it exists just as sugar exists permeated by sugarcane juice. || 13 ||
Pervaded by the nature of non-dual Brahman, I indeed encompass the three worlds; all living beings, from Brahmā down to the smallest insect, are conceived within me.
Just as a wave within the ocean undergoes transformations such as bubbles and the like, yet the ocean does not desire the fluidity residing in the wave; so it is here. (15)
May there be no desire for the pleasure of sense-objects in me, because I am of the nature of bliss; just as one who is wealthy has no hope for poverty, so it is with me.
For one who is immersed in the bliss of Brahman, there can be no desire for sense objects; having seen both poison and nectar, the wise man abandons the poison. || 17 ||
Having perceived the Self, I abandon even what is not the Self; the sun that illuminates a jar is not destroyed when the jar is destroyed.
The witness who illumines the body does not perish upon the destruction of the body. For me there is no bondage, no liberation, no scripture, and no teacher. (19)
Since I am the manifestation of mere illusion, I am beyond illusion and non-dual; let the vital breaths move with their attributes, or let the mind be struck down by desires.
How could there be suffering for me, who am filled with the consciousness of bliss? I know the Self directly; ignorance has fled somewhere.
Today my agency has perished, as has anything that ought to be done; likewise, my Brahminhood, my family, my lineage, my name, my beauty, and my caste [are gone]. (22)
All these—hunger, thirst, blindness, deafness, desire, anger, and so forth—which reside in the gross body, do not belong to me, who am distinct from the gross body. (23)

These qualities—insentience, pleasure, and delight—reside in the causal body; indeed, they do not exist in the one who is without a body (the *aliṅga*), though they are present in the subtle body (*liṅgadeha*).
For me, who am eternal and whose nature is changeless, these do not exist; just as darkness is perceived by an owl, though it does not exist for the sun.
Darkness arises for the deluded man regarding that which is self-luminous and supreme bliss; when the vision of the eyes is obstructed by clouds, one thinks, "The sun does not exist. (26)
Likewise, the embodied soul, veiled by ignorance, thinks "Brahman does not exist," just as nectar, though distinct from poison, is not tainted by the defects of poison. || 27 ||
Being distinct from the insentient, I do not touch the defects of the insentient due to my luminosity; even a tiny spark of a lamp can destroy a vast amount of darkness. || 28 ||
Even a very slight awakening destroys dense and abundant darkness; just as a snake does not exist in a rope throughout the three periods of time, so it is with me.
From egoity to the end of the body, the world does not exist; I am non-dual. Because my nature is consciousness, I have no insentience; because I am reality, there is no falsehood in me.

Because of its nature as bliss, there is no suffering for me; through ignorance, it appears as such, just as [the world appears real] to one who believes in the reality [of the dream]. Having meditated for even a moment upon this *Upāsanopaniṣad* of Self-awakening, one does not return again. "One does not return again"—this is the secret teaching (*upaniṣad*). 31.
Oṃ! "May my speech be in my mind"—thus [is] peace.
